   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: G.A.Jones, 63 Clare Ave.,
      Hoole, CHESTER CH2 3HR.

I noted your news on the Hobbit
plus the address of the supplier
and wrote the same night - SAE
as usual- but as yet, no answer!
I am now getting used to this
somewhat discourteous treatment
from the purveyors of computing
devices and must assume they are
all mad busy with orders and
customers. On second thoughts
more likely to be having trouble
over the ROM copyright with you
know who!

Ah well, I shall just have to
get on with building my bomb-
proof 48K. I have reached the
stage of having a keyboard with

real keys and now have to decide
how I can attach my various,
necessary, and (I hope)
compatible dongles, not least of
these the essential +D. In my
view they must be proof against
vibration, corrosion, the cat,
thermal creep, and lastly my
grandson. Might stick them all
in box, PSU, Speccy board, etc.
and stick a fan in the side like
a PC (I have got an old
DK'tronic's keyboard rigged like
that, and it is still going
strong).

I could put a drive in too.There
are a lot of FD9 cased drives
going around surplus at `25.00
if these can be persuaded to
operate on the +D I would be
keen, anybody out there know?

They are new and apparently used
to plug into the A-----d printer
port,3.5" and rated at 720K, but
according to my information they
are actually 1.44Mb. Studying my
data book of useless interfaces
the A-----d one seems to be very
similiar to the Speccy, only it
has 34 strips,mostly unconnected
8 data lines, 1 strobe, 1 busy
and 13 ground. The remaining 11
are not connected. I note the +D
has an equal number of pins.I've
searched all my back numbers of
Format but can't find the pinout
of the +D, yet again, does any-
body out there know?

Lastly, I noted your remarks on
PBT Electronics a while back. I
have been trying to contact them
for ages as I have a very sick

drive (hence my interest in
FD9's!) However,there is a short
note in the October issue of
Format to the effect that due to
a number of complaints, Format
are suspending their advert un-
til the position is clarified -
according to PBT it was due to
moving premises.

All my best wishes during your
fiscal troubles, being an OAP
I'm on the hit list too!At least
they can't close us down and try
to flood the workings! Feel free
to publish my address, going by
the volume of junk mail received
every con artist in the country
has got it anyway and who knows,
I might get some real feedback.

Best of luck,             - Geo.

Brian Cavers to George Jones

The +D pinouts are given by
Malcolm Perry in OUTLETTERS 60.

It's worth repeating again for
others: UNDER NO CIRCUMSTANCES
DEAL WITH PBT! We've been trying
all year to recover two machines
and a Disciple sent for repair.
PBT failed to answer all letters
and faxes. Trying to get through
on the phone has been impossible
and just a waste of time. We're
currently asking the police to
help recover the goods.

We've been told Paul Thomas of
PBT is"merely"incompetent rather
than "bent" but anyone running a
mail order business that way is
very suspect.           - Brian

Dear Brian,
The reason why you do not have a
label for 'the force that tends
to hurl objects outward in a
spinning centrifuge' - your
words - is that there is no such
force. OK - I can hear your
expression of incredulity
(politely expressed, I hope!)
from here, but bear with me and
I will try to explain. Before
doing so, however, two comments.
Firstly, I am talking about
motion in a circle - if we were
to look at what goes on when,
for example,you are whirling the
stone on the end of a string
about your head there are all
sorts of additional forces and
accelerations involved.

Secondly, you are driving me
into making dogmatic statements
in a way that appears to make me
out to be an 'expert' myself. I
make no such claim - hopefully I
am correctly inter- preting what
the real experts have said, no
more.

I am not sure exactly what you
mean by a centrifuge - one
possibility is, for example, the
device they use in a medical
context to separate solid and
liquid components in a test
tube, or else there is, for
example, the rotating beam at
RAE Farnborough - you may have
seen Helen Sharman on this in
the recent BBC1 broadcasts about
the Farnborough Air Show.


However, I think that there is a
simpler 'thought experiment'
that would lead you to argue
that there is a force throwing
you outwards, and I would like
to try it on you.

Suppose there is a large gramo-
phone turntable that you are
standing on. In reality the
question of what happens to you
depends upon friction between
the surface of the platter and
the soles of your shoes, but
friction can be quite complicat-
ed. Let me, therefore, simplify
yet again, and suppose that you
are wearing boots containing
electromagnets that are as
strong as necessary, that the
platter is ferro-magnetic, and
that it is frictionless.

Switch on your electromagnets,
and I will spin up the platter
to a steady state. Suppose then
that you switch off the magnets,
what happens? I dislike putting
words into other people's
mouths, but I suspect you would
say there is then a force that
throws you off the platter.

But consider: in the situation
where the magnets are switched
on I hope that my earlier letter
has convinced you that there is
a centripetal force acting on
you, making you move in a circle
and hence towards its centre,
rather than doing what Newton
says you really want to do, ie,
to go in a straight line. Then
why on earth (pun only just
noticed!) should this force turn

into a centrifugal force when
you switch off your magnets? -
and further, since there is no
friction, how does the platter
exert (horizontal) force on you?

The answer to this apparent dil-
emma,at least as I understand it
is that what really happens when
you switch off the magnets is
that you then travel in the
straight line that you always
preferred. Of course this means
you move towards the edge of the
platter and eventually fall off,
but this is not because of any
force exerted on you - it is
purely an effect of Newton's
first law. You might almost say
that you move forward in a
straight line and the platter
moves away from under you!

I suspect we have gone as far as
we can usefully do on 'Nanook':I
am happy to carry on the debate,
but I do not want to delay the
next OUTLET! If you want to call
a halt, then please do so.

A random thought. I know that,
in contrast to other numbers in
Spectrum/SAM BASIC, line numbers
are stored with the more signif-
icant part of the number first,
like humans do. But why? - I
cannot see any obvious reason
for this.

Another random comment.I recent-
ly had a get-together with Danny
Beach- he lives only a few miles
away from me - and we were comp-
aring notes on the current
OUTLET.

He takes the Spectrum version.
Both he and I were surprised,
albeit for opposite reasons, to
see that whereas the Spectrum
disk had 550k free (this is what
I remember: it could be slightly
inaccurate) the SAM one had 0k.
We did not have time to sort out
why - is it because of the over-
heads for the SAM style you use
or is there a real difference in
technical content?

You may remember that I raised
the question of what could be
called SUPERENUMBER ie a program
or procedure that could renumber
lines out of sequence. As has
happened before, writing to you
has inspired me to look at the
problem again, and I have made a
certain amount of progress.

Originally I was trying to put a
line into the EDITing area,alter
its line number and re-ENTER it.

However, looking for something
else,I came across an article by
David Threlfall in the February
1985 (No 11) edition of 'Your
Spectrum' about using BASIC ROM
routines from within a machine
code program, and this inspired
me to look at the use of various
ROM routines. The resulting
BASIC program, set out below,
demonstrates how far I have got.

All it does is to take one part-
icular line, 10, renumber it as
75, and then put it in the right
place in the listing.I have used
a BASIC program since...


(a) one is needed as a demon-
stration of the process in any
case, and

(b) because everyone can then
use it, even if they do not have
an assembler.

Clearly I need to wrap various
loops around this central act-
ivity to deal with more than one
line, and also do some error
checking. Even then, it does not
deal with the need to alter the
references to line numbers in
GOTO's etc. Still, it is some
progress, and it is offered to
your readers for comment:

I am not familiar enough with
ROM routines to be certain that
I have a fool-proof subroutine


that will work in all circum-
stances. Note that so far I have
only dealt with the Spectrum
since I do not have a good
enough picture of SAM's ROM (nor
an equivalent of Logan/O'Hara).
I wonder whether doing something
like this in the middle of a
running program may confuse SAM,
since I believe that SAM does
some preprocessing of the
program before RUnning it.

1   REM Demonstration of
   'SUPERENUMB', which can
    renumber BASIC lines out of
    sequence
2   REM all this program does is
    to shift line 10 to line 75
10  FOR n=65 TO 90:PRINT
    CHR$(n);:NEXT n:PRINT ':
    REM old line 10

20  FOR n=0 TO 55
25  READ a
30  POKE (40000+n),a
40  NEXT n
50  RANDOMIZE USR 40000
80  STOP
100 DATA 33,10,00:REM LD HL,10
110 DATA 205,110,25:REM CALL
    LINE-ADDR at &196E,which
    puts the address  of the
    start of line 10 into HL
115 DATA 229:REM stack a copy
    of the start address for
    future use
120 DATA 229,35,35,78,35,70,03,
    03,03,03,225,197:REM stack
    another copy of the start
    address, make BC equal to
    the total length of the
    line - the recorded 'length'
    does not include the two-


    byte line number or the two-
    byte length record itself -
    recover the address of the
    start of line 10 and stack
    the length of line 10 for
    future use
130 DATA 17,00,196,237,176:REM
    LD DE with the start of
    temporary working space
    at &C400 then do an LDIR
    to move line 10 there
133 DATA 193,225,197,205,232,
    25:REM recover the length
    of line 10 and its start
    address and then CALL
    RECLAIM-2 at &19E8, which
    effectively deletes line 10
    from the program
135 DATA 33,0,196,35,54,75:REM
    alter the line number of the
    line in temporary working
    space to 75

140 DATA 33,75,00,205,110,25:REM
    put 75, the new line number,
    into HL and then CALL
    LINE-ADDR again. Since in
    this case the line number
    does not exist (needs error
    checking) HL then contains
    the address of the start of
    the line whose line number
    is next after 75 - in this
    case line 100
150 DATA 193,197,229,205,85,22,
    209,193,33 ,00,196,237,176
    201: REM recover length of
    line 10, save it for future
    use, save address of start
    of line after line 75 for
    future use, CALL MAKE-ROOM
    at &1655 to open up the
    program to make room for the
    new line 75, recover the


    address of the start of the
    space for line 75 into DE,
    recover the  length  of  the
    line into BC , LD HL with
    &C400 then do an LDIR to
    copy the new line from temp
   into the space created for it
999 STOP

As ever with my programs, my
only claim is that it works. No
doubt there are more elegant
ways of doing the job - at one
stage I thought that I was back
using FORTH stacks and RPN! I
tried to use the ROM's own
workspace instead of the
temporary area I create at
&C400, but I could not get it to
work. I should welcome any
comments, either through the
letters columns or else direct.

All best wishes,

           Alan D.Cox

PS I must be slow - I have only
just realised, in relation to
LDIR, that DE are the first two
letters of destination!

Brian Cavers to Alan D. Cox

I follow what you say about the
forces acting on a rotating body
but there does APPEAR to be a
force pushing a body outwards in
rotation and this apparent force
is spoken of generally as the
"centrifugal force". You  will
find it in most dictionaries. I
agree with your analysis but it
may be that you you are simply
describing what centrifugal
force is - namely, the force or
pressure felt when the tendency
of a moving object to continue
in a straight line is being
restrained (by gravity or say,
the arm of a centrifuge). I'll
give in on this one though but I
reserve the right to use the
commonly-accepted expression.

You see, it may be possible to
show that the term "centrifugal"
is misused but most of us accept
the term and we all understand
ourselves by using the common
vocabulary. In fact, the term is
so widely accepted that one may
argue that the definition of the
word IS its common usage.

I concede you may be technically
correct (although I am still not
certain) but there really is an
impression of a force which most
accept is named "centrifugal"and
so whenever the expression is
used we all know what we mean.

I saw Helen Sharman and was most
impressed that she showed not a
trace of being subject to a huge
force of 7 times Earth gravity!

SAM high-res colour graphics use
up huge amounts of space on the
OUTLET disc even though they are
compressed. The Spectrum version
of OUTLET is also limited by the
size of the Opus disc (180K)
except for extras in ADD-ENDERS
and by editing time.

As for LDIR, yes - and HL stands
for home as well as high and low
while BC is "bytes counter"! I
wonder if this was chance or did
Zilog name them for this reason?
Probably so because G was missed
out completely.

Thanks for the listing but I do
think it makes more sense to
send the program itself to a
disc magazine!
                        - Brian.

yours?

From: E. Thomson, Suffolk



Dear Chezron,

Two things: Malcolm Goodman's
problem (Spectrum program) and
the "EASTER" calculator.

I use INPUT x$ to specify the
variable whose value is to be
given, so the already stored x$
must be copied somewhere. Since
Spectrum BASIC allows only one-
letter names for strings and
string arrays, and the name of a
string array can't be the same
as a string variable, the only
way I can think of is to use a
numerical array; it must have a

one-letter name, but this can be
the same as that of a numerical
variable.

I have to use a counting vari-
able, n, so the "real" value of
n must also be copied.


The routine proper starts at
Line 100, and, theoretically,
the variables a,b,...,z and
a$,b$,...,z$ have been given
values previously; the program
gives values to a few, so that
the routine can be tested.


[the program listed on the next
page is on the SAM OUTLET disc
in ADD-ENDERS as"MGPROBLEM" -Ed]

10 LET a=1:LET b=2:LET n=14: LET
   x=24
20 LET a$="alpha":LET b$="bravo"
   :Let x$="x-ray"
100 DIM n(2): LET n(1)=n: LET
    n(2)=LEN x$
110 DIM x(n(2))
120 FOR n=1 TO n(2):
    LET x(n)=CODE x$(n): NEXT n
130 INPUT "variable name:";x$
140 PRINT x$;":";
150 IF LEN x$=2 THEN GO TO 190
160 IF x$="n" THEN PRINT n(1)
170 IF x$<>"n" THEN PRINT VAL x$
180 GO TO 210
190IF x$<>"x$"THEN PRINT VAL$ x$
200 IF x$="x$" THEN GO SUB 300:
    PRINT x$
210 GO TO 130
300 LET x$="": FOR n=1 TO n(2)
310 LET x$=x$+CHR$ x(n): NEXT n
320 RETURN

In Alan Cox's program for calc-
ulating Easter (OUTLET 61, "More
Mail"), the year has to be 1583
onwards, which must be because
of the new calendar system
introduced by Pope Gregory in
October 1582, when 10 days were
"lost". This Gregorian system
was presumably adopted by Roman
Catholic countries, but not
everywhere. Britain did not
adopt it until September 1752,
when 11 days were lost, and
Russia waited until 1919. So if
you use this program for calc-
ulating Easter in Britain, a
year before 1753 would give the
wrong answer.
              Regards,

          Ettrick Thomson

From: S.M. Goodman, LEEDS

Dear Brian, Ron, and Averil,

Thanks once more for another
enjoyable OUTLET (Issue 62). I
echo the support offered by
other readers who feel that a
price rise would not be unreas-
onable. After all, one normally
looks forward to a pay increase
each year, and you should not be
excepted.

It's nice to see my "variables"
puzzle has had a response with
one or two elegant ideas, which
make my solution, (with you),
rather long-winded. Most solut-
ions seem to concentrate on pro-
cessing a given strong variable,

whereas my answer offers a num-
eric/string approach.Still, it's
good to see people rise to a
challenge. What a pity Sinclair
didn't provide for'long' strings
such as CHARLIE$ or help etc.
Had he done so the problem would
never (?) have arisen.

I went to the local All Formats
Fair here in Leeds last Sunday.
The hall was half empty and
apart from the 'Format' stand,
which appeared to be doing very
little whilst I was there, there
was no Spectrum/SAM support.

I met Bruce Everiss, briefly,
whilst he was dishing  out his
'`1.00 off' vouchers, which gave
me a chance to tell hilm that I
thought his admission price was

too high. However, I did find a
table where advance tickets
could be bought for `2.00 which
I feel is on the upper limit of
a realistic price.

Now onto a suggestion. As I
mentioned earlier. there was
little support for our 8 bit
machines and I wondered if there
was any mileage in approaching
the other regular 8 bit mag-
azines (Enceladus, Fred, Sam
Supplement, Format) to take a
stand on a cost-sharing basis,
so that your 'presence' wouuld
only cost `10 to `15 per show
instead of `60. So, you could be
present at Leicester with the
others products, someone else in
Scotland, and so on - and with
that thought I will close.

         Best Regards,

  Malcolm 'The Poser' Goodman

P.S. Hope you've got a good
solution!!

Cox, Pen-y-Maes, Ostrey Hill St Clears, Dyfed SA33 4AJ Dear Brian, The reason why you do not have a label for 'the force that tends to hurl objects outward in a spinning centrifuge' - your words - is that there is no such force. OK - I can hear your expression of incredulity (politely expressed, I hope!) from here, but bear with me and I will try to explain. Before doing so, however, two comments. Firstly, I am talking about motion in a circle - if we were to look at what goes on when, for example,you are whirling the stone on the end of a string about your head there are all sorts of additional forces and accelerations involved.

Secondly, you are driving me into making dogmatic statements in a way that appears to make me out to be an 'expert' myself. I make no such claim - hopefully I am correctly inter- preting what the real experts have said, no more.

I am not sure exactly what you mean by a centrifuge - one possibility is, for example, the device they use in a medical context to separate solid and liquid components in a test tube, or else there is, for example, the rotating beam at RAE Farnborough - you may have seen Helen Sharman on this in the recent BBC1 broadcasts about the Farnborough Air Show.

However, I think that there is a simpler 'thought experiment' that would lead you to argue that there is a force throwing you outwards, and I would like to try it on you.

Suppose there is a large gramo- phone turntable that you are standing on. In reality the question of what happens to you depends upon friction between the surface of the platter and the soles of your shoes, but friction can be quite complicat- ed. Let me, therefore, simplify yet again, and suppose that you are wearing boots containing electromagnets that are as strong as necessary, that the platter is ferro-magnetic, and that it is frictionless.

Switch on your electromagnets, and I will spin up the platter to a steady state. Suppose then that you switch off the magnets, what happens? I dislike putting words into other people's mouths, but I suspect you would say there is then a force that throws you off the platter.

But consider: in the situation where the magnets are switched on I hope that my earlier letter has convinced you that there is a centripetal force acting on you, making you move in a circle and hence towards its centre, rather than doing what Newton says you really want to do, ie, to go in a straight line. Then why on earth (pun only just noticed!) should this force turn

into a centrifugal force when you switch off your magnets? - and further, since there is no friction, how does the platter exert (horizontal) force on you?

The answer to this apparent dil- emma,at least as I understand it is that what really happens when you switch off the magnets is that you then travel in the straight line that you always preferred. Of course this means you move towards the edge of the platter and eventually fall off, but this is not because of any force exerted on you - it is purely an effect of Newton's first law. You might almost say that you move forward in a straight line and the platter moves away from under you!

Мне приходится использовать переменную цикла, n, поэтому «настоящее» значение n тоже нужно сохранить.

Собственно подпрограмма начинается со строки 100, и теоретически переменным a,b,...,z и a$,b$,...,z$ уже должны быть присвоены значения ранее; программа задает значения нескольким из них, чтобы алгоритм можно было протестировать.

[программа, приведенная ниже, находится на диске SAM OUTLET в разделе ADD-ENDERS под именем «MGPROBLEM» - Ред.]

```text
10 LET a=1:LET b=2:LET n=14: LET x=24
20 LET a$="alpha":LET b$="bravo":Let x$="x-ray"
100 DIM n(2): LET n(1)=n: LET n(2)=LEN x$
110 DIM x(n(2))
120 FOR n=1 TO n(2): LET x(n)=CODE x$(n): NEXT n
130 INPUT "variable name:";x$
140 PRINT x$;":";
150 IF LEN x$=2 THEN GO TO 190
160 IF x$="n" THEN PRINT n(1)
170 IF x$<>"n" THEN PRINT VAL x$
180 GO TO 210
190 IF x$<>"x$" THEN PRINT VAL$ x$
200 IF x$="x$" THEN GO SUB 300: PRINT x$
210 GO TO 130
300 LET x$="": FOR n=1 TO n(2)
310 LET x$=x$+CHR$ x(n): NEXT n
320 RETURN
```
